name: Common House Gecko
dangerNotes: Completely harmless. A welcome resident that eats mosquitoes and other insects.
description: The common house gecko is the most widespread and familiar gecko in Southeast Asia, found on the walls and ceilings of virtually every home, shop, and restaurant after dark. A supreme coloniser, it has spread across the tropics aboard cargo ships and now inhabits every continent except Antarctica. Its distinctive chirping call — 'chak chak chak' — is a defining sound of tropical nights across the region.
funFact: The common house gecko produces a distinctive chirping call used for communication — in many Southeast Asian cultures, counting the number of calls is considered an omen for good or bad luck.

name: Tokay Gecko
dangerNotes: Will bite hard and hold on if handled. Bite is painful but not dangerous. Can draw blood. Do not handle.
description: The tokay gecko is the largest gecko in Southeast Asia and one of the most recognisable, with a stocky blue-grey body covered in vivid orange-red spots. Its loud, distinctive two-syllable call — 'to-KAY, to-KAY' — booms through tropical nights and is responsible for its common name. A powerful predator of insects, small lizards, and even young rodents, it is highly territorial and will bite aggressively if disturbed.
funFact: The tokay gecko's bite force is extraordinary relative to its size — it can bite hard enough to draw blood and will clamp down and refuse to release, earning it a fearsome reputation among locals.

name: Asian Water Monitor
dangerNotes: Can bite and whip with its powerful tail — both are painful and the bite carries bacteria. Large adults are formidable. Do not corner or approach.
description: The Asian water monitor is the second heaviest lizard on Earth and one of the most adaptable reptiles in Southeast Asia, thriving in everything from pristine mangroves to city drains and rubbish dumps. A powerful swimmer, it hunts fish, crabs, carrion, eggs, and small mammals. Revered in some cultures and feared in others, it is an essential scavenger in both natural and urban ecosystems throughout the region.
funFact: The Asian water monitor is one of the few lizards known to actively scavenge human waste in cities — Bangkok's Lumphini Park is famous for its population of large individuals that treat park visitors with total indifference.

name: Green Crested Lizard
dangerNotes: Completely harmless.
description: The green crested lizard is a slender, long-tailed agamid with vivid emerald-green colouring and a distinctive serrated crest along neck and back. An arboreal species, it perches motionless on branches and tree trunks where its colouring provides near-perfect camouflage. When stressed it can turn brown or dark — the basis of the widespread but false belief that it is a chameleon. A swift, agile hunter of insects and small invertebrates.
funFact: The green crested lizard is often mistaken for a chameleon because it can shift from vivid green to dark brown when stressed — but unlike true chameleons, it has no special colour-change cells and does this through simple pigment redistribution.

name: Sun Skink
dangerNotes: Completely harmless. Will flee if approached.
description: The many-lined sun skink is one of the most commonly seen lizards across Southeast Asia, a robust, glossy-scaled skink that loves to bask in sunny patches on logs, rocks, and footpaths. Named for its habit of sunbathing, it has a brown back with pale lateral stripes and a copper-orange flush to the flanks. A quick, alert predator of insects and small invertebrates, it retreats rapidly into leaf litter or undergrowth at the first sign of danger.
funFact: Sun skinks are one of the few skink species in the region that give birth to live young rather than laying eggs — retaining developing embryos internally until they are fully formed.

name: Monocled Cobra
dangerNotes: Extremely dangerous. Potent neurotoxic and cytotoxic venom causes paralysis and tissue destruction — bites are frequently fatal without treatment. Spreads a broad hood when threatened. Seek emergency care immediately if bitten.
description: The monocled cobra is one of the most medically significant snakes in Southeast Asia, responsible for a large proportion of serious snakebite cases across the region. Named for the distinctive O-shaped or monocle marking on the back of its hood, it inhabits agricultural land, forest edges, and is regularly found near villages. Unlike the spitting cobra, it does not spit venom, but its bite delivers a potent combination of neurotoxins and cytotoxins.
funFact: The monocled cobra's distinctive hood marking — a single O-shaped 'eye' on the back — is thought to function as a false face to confuse and deter predators approaching from behind.

name: Reticulated Python
dangerNotes: The world's longest snake — adults regularly exceed 5 metres and have killed humans by constriction. Never approach large individuals alone. Even mid-sized adults are capable of serious injury. Back away and do not provoke.
description: The reticulated python is the world's longest snake, with verified individuals exceeding 6 metres and unverified records beyond 8. Its intricate golden, black, and white geometric patterning — the 'reticulation' — gives it its name. Supremely adaptable, it inhabits rainforest, mangroves, and urban drains alike, and is a regular visitor to suburban areas across Southeast Asia. A powerful ambush predator, it has on rare occasions killed and swallowed adult humans.
funFact: The reticulated python holds the record for the world's longest snake — a specimen from Indonesia measured at 7.67 metres, and local accounts of individuals exceeding 8 metres are considered credible.

name: Oriental Whip Snake
dangerNotes: Rear-fanged and mildly venomous but not medically significant to humans. Bites are very rare. Harmless in practice.
description: The oriental whip snake is an extraordinarily slender arboreal snake, so thin relative to its length that it resembles a green vine or tendril hanging among foliage. Vivid lime-green with a pointed snout, it moves slowly and deliberately through vegetation hunting lizards and frogs. It has horizontally keyhole-shaped pupils that give it excellent binocular vision — unusually precise for a snake — allowing it to judge distance when striking from a branch.
funFact: The oriental whip snake has keyhole-shaped horizontal pupils that give it binocular depth perception — one of the very few snakes capable of genuinely judging distance, a crucial adaptation for striking at prey from branches.

name: Crab-eating Macaque
dangerNotes: Can bite and scratch. Carries Herpes B virus (potentially fatal to humans). Highly opportunistic — will snatch food, bags, and glasses. Do not feed. Do not make eye contact with dominant males.
description: The crab-eating macaque, also known as the long-tailed macaque, is the most commonly encountered primate across Southeast Asia — ubiquitous at temples, beach resorts, forest parks, and coastal areas. Despite its name, it eats almost anything: crabs, fruit, insects, small animals, and human food. Highly intelligent and socially complex, it lives in troops with rigid dominance hierarchies. Its boldness and adaptability have made it both a cultural icon and an urban nuisance.
funFact: Crab-eating macaques in Thailand and Myanmar have been observed using stone tools to crack open shellfish and nuts — one of the few non-ape primates documented using tools in the wild.

name: Asian Palm Civet
dangerNotes: Nocturnal and reclusive. Will scratch and bite if cornered. Otherwise avoids humans.
description: The Asian palm civet is a small, cat-like carnivore with a dark grizzled coat, black mask, and pale-spotted flanks. Highly adaptable, it thrives in forest, plantation, and suburban environments across Southeast Asia. Primarily frugivorous, it plays an important role in seed dispersal. It is also, controversially, the source of kopi luwak — coffee made from beans passed through its digestive system — the world's most expensive coffee.
funFact: The Asian palm civet is responsible for kopi luwak, the world's most expensive coffee — it eats ripe coffee cherries and the beans, partially digested and fermented in its gut, are collected, cleaned, and sold for up to $700 per kilogram.

name: Common Treeshrew
dangerNotes: Completely harmless. Extremely shy and fast — rarely seen closely.
description: The common treeshrew resembles a small squirrel with a pointed snout, but is not a rodent — it belongs to the order Scandentia, considered one of the closest living relatives of primates. Hyperactive and diurnal, it dashes along branches and forest floors at high speed, foraging for insects, fruit, and small vertebrates. Despite its name, it spends much of its time on the ground. Its remarkably high metabolic rate means it must eat almost constantly.
funFact: Treeshrews have the highest brain-to-body-mass ratio of any mammal — higher even than humans — though this reflects their tiny body size rather than exceptional intelligence.

name: Sunda Flying Lemur
dangerNotes: Completely harmless. Nocturnal and arboreal — very rarely encountered.
description: The Sunda flying lemur — also called the colugo — is neither a lemur nor capable of true flight, but its gliding membrane (patagium) stretches from its chin to the tips of its fingers, toes, and tail, giving it the most complete gliding surface of any gliding mammal. It can glide over 136 metres between trees with minimal altitude loss. Despite its superficial resemblance to lemurs, it is most closely related to primates — our nearest non-primate relative.
funFact: The Sunda flying lemur can glide over 136 metres in a single leap with a height loss of less than 10 metres — a gliding efficiency that exceeds flying squirrels and rivalled only by true bats among nocturnal mammals.

name: Asian Elephant
dangerNotes: Extremely dangerous. Elephants kill hundreds of people per year across Asia. Bulls in musth are especially unpredictable and lethal. Mothers with calves will charge without warning. Never approach, block an escape route, or get between a mother and her calf.
description: The Asian elephant is the largest land animal in Asia and one of the most intelligent creatures on Earth, with a complex social structure, long-term memory, and documented self-awareness. Smaller than the African elephant with distinctively smaller ears and a domed head, it lives in matriarchal family groups led by the oldest female. In Thailand it holds deep cultural and spiritual significance, serving historically as a war animal, working animal, and national symbol.
funFact: Asian elephants are one of the few animals that demonstrate self-awareness — individuals recognise themselves in mirrors, a cognitive ability shared only with great apes, dolphins, and a handful of other species.

name: Oriental Pied Hornbill
dangerNotes: No threat to humans.
description: The oriental pied hornbill is the smallest and most widespread hornbill in Southeast Asia, with bold black-and-white plumage and a large yellow-and-black casque atop its bill. Famous for its extraordinary nesting behaviour: the female seals herself inside a tree cavity using mud and droppings, leaving only a narrow slit through which the male passes food, until the chicks are ready to fledge. A noisy, social bird, its loud cackling calls are characteristic of forest edges and offshore islands.
funFact: Female hornbills seal themselves inside tree hollows during nesting — entombed with their eggs and then chicks for up to four months while the male feeds them through a narrow slit, making them entirely dependent on their partner's fidelity.

name: White-throated Kingfisher
dangerNotes: No threat to humans.
description: The white-throated kingfisher is one of the most conspicuous and boldly coloured birds of Southeast Asia, with a vivid turquoise back and wings, chestnut head and flanks, and a brilliant white throat and breast. Unusually for a kingfisher, it hunts far from water — perching on telephone wires, fence posts, and roof edges to dive on lizards, large insects, frogs, and even small rodents. Its loud, laughing call is a defining sound of the tropical dawn.
funFact: Despite being called a kingfisher, the white-throated kingfisher often lives far from water and regularly hunts lizards, insects, and rodents in dry urban gardens — it is named for its family, not its diet.

name: Collared Kingfisher
dangerNotes: No threat to humans.
description: The collared kingfisher is one of the most widespread kingfishers in the world, ranging from the Red Sea to the Pacific. In Southeast Asia it is a constant presence in mangroves, coastal parks, and urban gardens. Blue-green above with a crisp white collar and underparts, it hunts from a prominent perch, diving on crabs, mudskippers, lizards, and large insects. Its loud, harsh 'kek-kek-kek' call rings out constantly across mangrove-fringed coastlines.
funFact: The collared kingfisher has one of the widest distributions of any kingfisher in the world — 49 recognised subspecies spread from the Red Sea coast to the islands of the Pacific Ocean.

name: Asian Koel
dangerNotes: No threat to humans.
description: The Asian koel is one of the most heard but rarely seen birds of Southeast Asia. The male is glossy jet black with a vivid red eye; the female is beautifully streaked brown. A brood parasite, the koel lays its eggs in the nests of crows and other large birds, leaving the hosts to raise its chicks. The male's rising, repetitive 'ko-el' call — accelerating in pitch through the dawn hours — is an iconic and sometimes maddening sound of tropical cities.
funFact: The Asian koel's call has been scientifically proven to accelerate in tempo and pitch over the breeding season — a vocal performance that can begin before dawn and continue relentlessly for hours, making it both beloved and infamous in equal measure.

name: Oriental Magpie-Robin
dangerNotes: No threat to humans.
description: The oriental magpie-robin is one of the finest songbirds in Southeast Asia — a small, bold black-and-white bird that delivers an extraordinarily rich and varied song from exposed perches, often at dawn. Males have a glossy blue-black head and back with white underparts and wing patches; females are grey-brown. Highly territorial, males sing persistently throughout the breeding season. It is the national bird of Bangladesh and deeply familiar across urban Southeast Asia.
funFact: The oriental magpie-robin is one of the most accomplished songbirds in Asia — males can produce over 50 distinct song phrases and frequently incorporate imitations of other species into their dawn chorus.

name: Olive-backed Sunbird
dangerNotes: No threat to humans.
description: The olive-backed sunbird is the most widespread and commonly seen sunbird in Southeast Asia, a tiny, restless nectarivore with an olive-green back and sulphur-yellow underparts. Males have a brilliant iridescent blue-black throat and breast. It hovers briefly or clings acrobatically to flowers to feed on nectar, and is an important pollinator across the region. It builds a distinctive hanging, pendulous nest of grass and spiders' webs suspended from branches or even laundry lines.
funFact: The olive-backed sunbird will happily build its hanging, pendulous nest from a washing line, a light fitting, or a clothes hanger — making it one of the most urban-adapted nesting birds in Southeast Asia.

name: Black-naped Oriole
dangerNotes: No threat to humans.
description: The black-naped oriole is a strikingly beautiful bird — vivid golden yellow with a black mask and nape band. One of the most conspicuous garden birds across urban Southeast Asia, it is often seen in fruiting trees and flowering canopy. Its rich, fluting whistle is one of the most melodious and instantly recognisable bird calls in the region. Adaptable to urban environments, it nests in a woven cup suspended hammock-like from a high branch.
funFact: The black-naped oriole's fluting call is one of the most melodious sounds in Southeast Asian gardens — it can be confused with a human whistling, and individuals are known to incorporate other bird calls and even human-made sounds into their song.

name: Blue-tailed Bee-eater
dangerNotes: No threat to humans.
description: The blue-tailed bee-eater is a vivid, acrobatic bird with green plumage, a rufous-orange throat, blue tail streamers, and a long decurved bill. It hunts bees, wasps, dragonflies, and other flying insects with spectacular aerial precision, catching them in mid-air and returning to a perch to beat and de-venom prey before swallowing. A gregarious, migratory species, it breeds in sandy banks and open ground and is a seasonal visitor across much of Southeast Asia.
funFact: Blue-tailed bee-eaters catch bees and wasps mid-flight then thrash them against a branch to remove the sting and squeeze out the venom sac before eating — a learned behaviour that prevents envenomation.

name: Brahminy Kite
dangerNotes: No threat to humans on the ground. May swoop if nesting nearby.
description: The brahminy kite is one of the most beautiful raptors in Southeast Asia — a medium-sized bird of prey with a pure white head and chest contrasting vividly with rich chestnut-red wings and back. A coastal and wetland specialist, it soars effortlessly over harbours, estuaries, and fishing villages, snatching dead fish, crabs, and carrion from the water surface. In Hindu mythology it represents Garuda, the vehicle of the god Vishnu.
funFact: The brahminy kite is considered a manifestation of the Hindu deity Garuda across much of Southeast Asia — it is a sacred bird in Bali, where it is believed to carry messages from the gods.

name: Black-shouldered Kite
dangerNotes: No threat to humans.
description: The black-shouldered kite is a small, elegant raptor with pale grey-white plumage, jet black shoulder patches, and striking red eyes. It hunts by hovering in place over open grassland — facing into the wind and scanning the ground below with exceptional eyesight before dropping onto rodents and large insects. Increasingly common across agricultural Southeast Asia, it benefits from open farmland where it is a highly effective rat predator.
funFact: The black-shouldered kite can hover almost perfectly stationary against the wind, maintaining position for up to a minute using tiny, rapid wingbeats and tail adjustments — a hunting technique called 'kiting'.

name: Sun Conure
dangerNotes: No threat to humans. Wild SEA populations are escaped captive birds.
description: The sun conure is a brilliantly coloured parrot native to northeastern South America, with vivid golden-yellow plumage shading to orange-red on the face and green on the wings. In Southeast Asia all wild individuals are escaped or released captive birds — the species is not native to the region. Highly social and extremely noisy, escaped flocks have established themselves in urban parks across Malaysia, Singapore, and Thailand. In its native range it is endangered due to trapping for the pet trade.
funFact: Every sun conure seen in the wild across Southeast Asia is descended from escaped or released pets — the species is not native to Asia but has established feral flocks in several major cities.

name: Rose-ringed Parakeet
dangerNotes: No threat to humans. Noisy in large flocks.
description: The rose-ringed parakeet is a long-tailed green parrot with a distinctive red bill and, in males, a black-and-rose neck ring. One of the most successful introduced birds in the world, it has established wild populations across Europe, the Middle East, and Southeast Asia from escaped cage birds. Intelligent, adaptable, and noisy, feral flocks roost communally in large numbers and can be agricultural pests. In Southeast Asia both native and introduced populations exist.
funFact: The rose-ringed parakeet is one of the most invasive bird species on Earth — escaped cage birds have established self-sustaining wild populations in over 35 countries, including the UK, where London now has over 12,000 wild individuals.

name: Red-breasted Parakeet
dangerNotes: No threat to humans.
description: The red-breasted parakeet is one of the most attractive parakeets in Southeast Asia, with grey-green plumage, a salmon-pink breast, black chin stripe, and red upper bill. It inhabits forest, plantations, and increasingly urban areas. Males and females are distinguishable — females have a dull reddish lower mandible while males have red upper and black lower. Highly gregarious, it roosts and forages in noisy, fast-flying flocks and is a popular cage bird.
funFact: The red-breasted parakeet can be reliably sexed by bill colour alone — males have a red upper mandible with black lower, while females have a fully dull reddish bill on both upper and lower.

name: Banded Bay Cuckoo
dangerNotes: No threat to humans.
description: The banded bay cuckoo is a small, secretive cuckoo with rufous-brown upperparts and a finely barred white underside. A brood parasite like its relatives, it lays its eggs in the nests of babblers and other small birds, whose own chicks it displaces. Heard far more often than seen, its distinctive plaintive, descending four-note whistle is a characteristic sound of Southeast Asian forest edges during the breeding season.
funFact: Cuckoo chicks hatch earlier than their hosts' own eggs and instinctively eject all other eggs from the nest within hours of hatching — blind, naked, and just hours old, they perform this behaviour with remarkable precision.

name: Greater Coucal
dangerNotes: No threat to humans.
description: The greater coucal is a large, crow-sized member of the cuckoo family with glossy blue-black plumage and rich chestnut-red wings. Unlike most cuckoos, it raises its own young rather than parasitising other birds. A slow, heavy bird that prefers to walk through dense undergrowth, it hunts lizards, large insects, eggs, and small rodents. Its deep, resonant 'boop-boop-boop' call is one of the most characteristic sounds of rural Southeast Asia.
funFact: Unlike most of its cuckoo relatives, the greater coucal builds its own nest and raises its own young — making it one of the few members of the cuckoo family that is not a brood parasite.

name: Spotted Dove
dangerNotes: No threat to humans.
description: The spotted dove is one of the most familiar and widespread birds of urban Southeast Asia, a pinkish-brown dove with a distinctive black-and-white spotted neck patch. It walks calmly on the ground foraging for seeds, completely untroubled by human presence. Its gentle, repetitive cooing — 'coo-coo-coo-coo' — is a constant background sound of tropical gardens and city parks. Introduced to Australia, Hawaii, and many other regions, it has become an established alien species.
funFact: Spotted doves, like all pigeons and doves, produce 'crop milk' — a protein-rich secretion from the lining of the crop that both parents feed to newly hatched squabs before they can digest solid food.

name: Zebra Dove
dangerNotes: No threat to humans.
description: The zebra dove is a tiny, delicately barred dove with fine black-and-white streaking on its neck and breast that resembles a zebra's stripes — giving it its name. One of the most abundant birds in urban Southeast Asia, it walks along pavements, garden paths, and outdoor café tables with total confidence. Its soft, rapid cooing is one of the most soothing sounds of the tropical dawn. It is extremely popular as a caged songbird in Thailand and Malaysia.
funFact: The zebra dove is so prized as a caged songbird in Thailand and Malaysia that competitive calling contests are held, with champion birds worth thousands of dollars — judges score their distinctive rapid cooing on duration, tone, and rhythm.
